title: The recipe nobody asked you to change
hook: Pepsi keeps winning the taste test. Do you change the world's most famous recipe?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: How much cola you sell today

future.label: Loyalty
future.hint: How much your fans love and trust Coke

intro.text: Atlanta, 1984. You run Coca-Cola, the best-known drink in the world, made almost the same way for nearly 100 years. But for 15 years in a row your lead over Pepsi has been shrinking, and your board wants you to stop the slide.

s_challenge.text: Since 1975, Pepsi has run the Pepsi Challenge in shops and malls. People sip two colas without seeing the names, and more of them pick Pepsi. When your own team runs blind tests, it gets the same answer: people prefer a sweeter taste.

d1.title: Why are we losing?
d1.setup: There is some good news. Diet Coke, launched in 1982, shows that new drinks can still win buyers. While making it, your lab also found a sweeter recipe that beat both Pepsi and your own Coke in tests.
d1.question: How do you stop the slide?
d1.advisor: Pepsi says the problem is our taste, and the tests agree. But changing the taste or starting a price war is hard to undo.

options.label: Work in secret on a sweeter recipe for Coke. It means changing a 99-year-old drink.
options.outcome: You decide taste is the problem. A secret team, code-named Project Kansas, works on a sweeter formula, and in tests with nearly 200,000 people it beats both Pepsi and the old Coke.
options.why: Testing new tastes is fair. But people buy Coke for habit and memories too, not only for one sip. Your team was now set on changing the main drink.
options.better: Keep the old recipe safe. Win with new drinks and fresh ads, the way Diet Coke did, and test new tastes as extra drinks.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you treated a fight about feelings as a fight about flavour.

options.label: Keep the recipe, and compete with new drinks and fresh ads. Progress will be slow.
options.outcome: You leave the recipe alone and put your money into new drinks and fresh ads. Progress is slow, but your fans keep the taste they grew up with, and Diet Coke keeps winning new buyers.
options.why: Your recipe was not your only strength. Your name, your history and your fans' habits were worth more than one sip in a blind test.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you grew around your core product instead of changing it.

options.label: Cut prices, so families get more Coke for their money. You will earn less on every can.
options.outcome: Cheaper Coke wins back some buyers, until Pepsi cuts its prices too. Now both of you earn less on every can, and the slide has not stopped.
options.why: A price war hurts both sides, and the stronger brand loses the most. It also tells fans your drink is worth less.
options.better: Protect your price. Give people new reasons to choose Coke, like new drinks and fresh ads.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you fought with discounts and made your own drink look cheap.

d2.title: The taste test winner

setup.text: The sweeter formula has won your tests. But the tests measured taste, not how people would feel if their old Coke disappeared, and about 10 to 12 in every 100 testers said they were angry at the very idea of a change.

Your new drinks are selling, but Pepsi is still close behind, and your marketing team wants to use the lab's sweeter recipe. In early tests, a few people say they would be angry if the old Coke changed.

The price war has left you with thin profits and no clear win, so your marketing team wants to use the lab's sweeter recipe. In early tests, a few people say they would be angry if the old Coke changed.

d2.question: What do you do with the new recipe?
d2.advisor: One Coke gives you one clear message, and the new taste wins the tests. But people have drunk the old one all their lives.

options.label: Launch the new taste as a second drink. Two Cokes could split your fans.
options.outcome: The sweet drink goes on shelves beside the old Coke. Pepsi gets no story about angry Coke fans, and your fans still have the drink they love.
options.why: You got the upside of the new taste without taking anything away from your fans.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you added a new choice instead of taking away an old one.

options.label: Replace the old Coke everywhere. One Coke, one message, and the taste that wins.

outcome.text: On April 23, 1985, at an event in New York, you announce the first new formula in 99 years, and the old recipe comes off the market. Pepsi gives its staff a day off and runs full-page newspaper ads.
You announce the new formula and take the old Coke off the market. Pepsi celebrates with newspaper ads, and reporters start asking your fans how they feel.

options.why: You took away something millions of people loved, and you trusted a sip test more than their feelings. The warning signs were in your own research.
options.better: Sell the new taste as an extra drink, or test it in a few cities first, and never take the old one away.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you took away what fans loved because a test said they would like something else.

options.label: Try it in a few cities first. It's slower, and Pepsi will see it coming.
options.outcome: In a few test cities, the sweet drink takes the old Coke's place. Within weeks, those cities send you a pile of angry letters, and the newspapers soon hear about it.
options.why: Testing first was careful. But in those cities you still took away the drink fans loved.
options.better: Launch the new taste as an extra drink, so nobody has to lose the old one.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tested before going big, but still tested the wrong idea.

d3.title: The fans fight back

setup.text: By June your hotline gets 1,500 calls a day, up from 400. In all, fans send about 40,000 letters. Fans form protest groups, people buy up all the old Coke they can find, and a poll says only 13 in 100 soda drinkers like the new taste.
Within weeks, your phones are ringing all day and the letters won't stop. Fans form protest groups and buy up all the old Coke they can find.

d3.question: Your fans are furious. What do you do?
d3.advisor: If we back down, the world will say we failed. If we stay the course, how many fans will we lose?

options.label: Spend big on ads for the new taste. People liked it in the tests; they need time.
options.outcome: You pour money into ads for the new taste. A few people switch, but most fans feel you are not listening, and the protests get louder.
options.why: Ads can tell people about a product. They cannot make people stop missing something they loved.
options.better: Admit the mistake fast. Bring the old recipe back and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tried to out-shout your own customers.

options.label: Tweak the new recipe to taste closer to the old one, and keep one Coke. It takes months.
options.outcome: Your lab works all summer on a softer version of the new taste. But fans don't want a closer copy of their Coke, they want the real one back, and some switch to Pepsi for good.
options.why: Fans weren't asking for a better new taste. They wanted the old one back, and every month in the lab made them angrier.
options.better: Listen to what fans are asking for. Bring the old recipe back quickly and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept fixing the new recipe when fans wanted the old drink back.

options.label: Bring back the old recipe and say sorry. The whole world will see you admit a mistake.

outcome.text: On July 11, 1985, just 79 days after the change, you say sorry and bring back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic. TV news breaks into regular shows to report it, and your hotline gets 31,600 calls in two days.
Within weeks of the change, you say sorry and bring the old recipe back. The news spreads fast, and your phones fill with calls from happy fans.

options.why: Saying sorry is hard for a big company. But you listened, moved within weeks, and gave fans back what they loved.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you admitted a big mistake fast and fixed it.

d3alt.title: What the test told you

setup.text: The sweet drink sits next to the old Coke. Some people like it, but most still reach for the taste they grew up with, and your sales team says two Cokes confuse shoppers.
In your test cities, many fans are angry that their old Coke is gone, while others like the sweet taste. Your team is split on what that means for the rest of the country.

d3alt.question: What next for the sweet recipe?
d3alt.advisor: The test gave us an answer. Now we have to decide what that answer means for the business.

options.label: Put the new taste everywhere anyway. Most testers liked it, and one Coke is simpler.

outcome.text: Fans across the country get angry, just as your test cities warned. After a hard summer of protests, you give in and bring the old taste back.
When the old Coke disappears, fans across the country get angry. After a hard summer of protests, you give in and bring the old taste back.

options.why: You had a warning and ignored it. A test is only useful if you act on what it tells you.
options.better: Keep the old Coke as the star, and sell the sweet taste only as a side drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you ignored your own warning signs.

options.label: Sell it only where buyers liked it. Running different Cokes costs more.
options.outcome: The sweet drink sells in a few places, but running different Cokes in different places is costly and confusing, and nobody is sure which Coke is the real one.
options.why: It limited the risk, but it split your effort for a small gain.
options.better: Make the old Coke the star everywhere, and keep the sweet taste as a clear side drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you played safe, but made your brand more confusing.

options.label: Keep the old Coke as the star, and sell the sweet one beside it as a small extra.

outcome.text: The old Coke goes back on the shelves in your test cities, with the sweet drink beside it. Fans calm down, and the sweet drink finds its own small group of buyers.
Fans keep the Coke they love, and the sweet drink finds its own small group of buyers. Slowly, your lead over Pepsi starts to grow again.

options.why: You listened to what the test really said: people liked the new taste, but loved the old Coke.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept your core safe and let the new idea earn its place.

text.text: Fans cheer, and Classic flies off the shelves. Now two Cokes sit side by side: Classic, and the new, sweeter drink, which still carries the name Coca-Cola.
Fans cheer, and the old Coke flies off the shelves again. Now two Cokes sit side by side: the old one, and the new, sweeter drink.

By late summer the tweaked recipe has changed few minds, and the protests won't stop. You finally bring the old recipe back, but fans say you only listened when you had no choice. Now two Cokes share the shelf.
The ads cost a fortune and change few minds. By late summer you bring the old recipe back, and now two Cokes share the shelf.
The old taste is back after a hard summer, and now two Cokes share the shelf. Many fans still haven't forgiven you.
In some towns shoppers find one Coke, and in others they find two. Your sales team wants one clear plan for the whole country.
The old Coke is still the star, and the sweet drink has a small group of fans. Pepsi is no longer gaining on you.

d4.title: Two Cokes on one shelf
d4.setup: Your ad money and your shelf space are limited, and both drinks want them. Whatever you back now will shape what people think Coke is.
d4.question: How do you run two colas at once?
d4.advisor: Two drinks can give you two chances, but they can also make the brand harder to understand.

options.label: Make the old Coke the star, and let the new drink fade. You admit the new taste failed.
options.outcome: You put your money behind the taste your fans chose, and the new drink quietly fades away. Shoppers know exactly which Coke is the real one.
options.why: You put your effort where your fans already were, and stopped spending on a drink they did not want.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you backed what your customers chose, not what you hoped they would choose.

options.label: Keep both, and give each its own big ad campaign. It costs twice as much.

outcome.text: You keep both drinks and give each its own ad campaign. Classic quickly outsells the new drink, and within a few months it is again the top sugar cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink falls to about 3% of the market.
You keep both drinks and give each its own ad campaign. The old taste outsells the new one by far, and much of your ad money goes to a drink few people want.

options.why: Keeping both limited the risk, but you spent money and attention on a drink few people wanted.
options.better: Put your weight behind the taste fans chose, and let the new drink fade quietly.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you split your effort between a winner and a loser.

options.label: Keep the new drink as your main Coke. Young people like sweeter colas, and Pepsi is winning them.
options.outcome: You back the new drink again. Fans feel ignored for a second time, and many of them decide Pepsi is the easier choice.
options.why: Chasing young Pepsi drinkers made sense on paper, but your own fans had already told you twice which Coke they wanted.
options.better: Back the drink your fans chose, and let the new one fade.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept pushing a product your customers had already rejected.

text.text: You never took your fans' favourite drink away. New drinks and fresh ads bring in new buyers, and Coke's lead over Pepsi grows again without a summer of anger.
You listened to what the test really said. The old Coke stays the star, the sweet drink stays a small extra, and Coke's lead over Pepsi grows again.
You made mistakes, but you listened quickly and backed the taste your fans loved. Coke ends the year stronger than Pepsi, and its fans know you will listen.

By the end of 1985, Coca-Cola Classic is selling well ahead of both the new drink and Pepsi. The new drink is later renamed Coke II and dropped in 2002, and in 2009 the word Classic comes off the label in North America. Coca-Cola comes out of the mess stronger.
The old Coke is back and selling again, but it took you a whole summer to listen. Coke stays ahead of Pepsi, and fans remember how long you made them wait.
You backed the wrong drink at the end, and some fans drift to Pepsi. Coke is still big and still ahead, but its lead is smaller than before the new drink.
You made some costly moves, but you listened in time. Your fans stay with you, and Coke stays ahead of Pepsi.

collapse.title: The cola that lost its fans

text.text: You pushed the new drink even after fans said no twice. Many of them switch to Pepsi for good, and the world's best-known drink loses its lead.
By the time you backed the taste your fans loved, too many of them had switched to Pepsi for good. The world's best-known drink loses its lead.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: Three costly calls are too many. The board has lost its trust in you, and it asks someone else to win the fans back.

realHistory: Coca-Cola was losing ground to Pepsi, which kept winning blind taste tests. After tests with nearly 200,000 people, it replaced its 99-year-old recipe with a sweeter one on April 23, 1985. Fans were furious, and calls, letters and protest groups poured in. After 79 days, on July 11, 1985, the company said sorry and brought back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic. Within months Classic was again the top sugar cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink fell to about 3% of the market and was dropped in 2002.
